# Detection-Gated Adaptive Region-of-Interest Reconstruction for single-lens infrared computational imaging

Author links open overlay panel Guishuo Yang ^{a} ^{b} ^{c} ^{1}, Yujie Xing ^{a} ^{b} ^{c} ^{1}, Xuanyu Qian ^{a} ^{b} ^{c}, Dongdong Li ^{a} ^{b} ^{c}, Kai Zhang ^{d} ^{e}, Shiyao Guo ^{a} ^{b} ^{c}, Xuquan Wang ^{a} ^{b} ^{c}, Xiong Dun ^{a} ^{b} ^{c}, Jiande Sun ^{d} ^{e}

10.1016/j.iopt.2026.100035

  * Article

## Abstract

Single-lens infrared imaging provides a compact alternative for resource-constrained platforms, but optical simplification inevitably leads to image degradation. Existing pipelines typically reconstruct the entire degraded frame before detection, which introduces unnecessary computation in target-sparse infrared scenes. To address this issue, we propose Detection-Gated Adaptive Region-of-Interest Reconstruction (DG-ROI Recon), a target-oriented framework for low-latency single-lens infrared computational imaging. The proposed method first performs detection on the degraded single-lens infrared image and uses the resulting bounding boxes as task-driven gates for subsequent reconstruction. According to the target scale, each box is assigned to an adaptive reconstruction bucket, followed by centered ROI cropping and local reconstruction. Target-relevant regions are selectively restored, while background regions are largely preserved to avoid redundant full-frame reconstruction. For large targets beyond the predefined bucket range, the framework falls back to full-frame reconstruction to ensure robustness. A halo-aware blending strategy is further introduced to suppress boundary artifacts between reconstructed ROIs and the degraded background. Experimental results show that the proposed DG-ROI Recon reduces inference time by 38.9% compared with full-frame reconstruction and by 62.8% compared with the conventional reconstruct-then-detect pipeline, while maintaining comparable ROI-level image quality.

Decoupling color and structure via dual-branch learning for high-fidelity underwater image restoration☆

Author links open overlay panel Haotian Sun ^{a}, Linlin Qi ^{b}, Tao Liu ^{b}

10.1016/j.oceaneng.2026.128196

## Highlights

  * •

A dual-branch RGB-grayscale network decouples color and structure.

  * •

An ERB with wavelet-based bypass enhances high-frequency details.

  * •

A Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion Module fuses cross-domain features.

  * •

Achieves competitive performance with 0.499M parameters and 72 FPS.

## Abstract

Underwater image restoration is severely challenged by simultaneous color distortion and detail degradation. Existing single-branch methods inherently entangle color and structure, struggling to balance chromatic correction with structural recovery. To fundamentally resolve this optimization conflict, we propose the Underwater Dual-branch High-frequency Enhancement Network (UDHE), which explicitly decouples these two aspects via parallel RGB-grayscale learning. The grayscale branch provides structural and illumination priors free from chromatic biases, effectively isolating structural recovery from chromatic correction. Specifically, we design three core innovations: an Efficient Residual Block (ERB) with a wavelet-based frequency bypass for explicit high-frequency compensation, a Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) module for semantic-guided multi-scale alignment, and a Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion Module (BDFM) with mutual attention and dynamic gating for adaptive cross-domain feature integration. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that UDHE achieves superior performance. On the UIEB-T90 benchmark, our method attains a PSNR of 23.97 dB and SSIM of 0.9154, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art approaches, while maintaining high efficiency with only 0.499M parameters and an inference speed of 72 FPS. Code is available at: https://github.com/Qlinlin/UDHE.

## Introduction

Underwater image enhancement (UIE) has emerged as a fundamental low-level vision task due to its critical role in marine exploration, underwater robotics, and autonomous subaquatic navigation (Ding et al., 2024, Sultan et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025). The quality of underwater visual data directly affects the accuracy and efficiency of downstream operations such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and visual SLAM (Xu et al., 2023, Islam et al., 2020a, Zhang et al., 2022). However, images captured in underwater environments typically suffer from severe degradation caused by wavelength-dependent light absorption and scattering. These physical phenomena lead to color distortion, contrast reduction, blurring, and loss of fine details, with the severity varying across depth, water turbidity, and lighting conditions (Raveendran et al., 2021).

Traditional UIE methods can be broadly categorized into three groups. Classical image processing techniques such as histogram equalization (Pizer et al., 1987) and Retinex-based models operate directly in the pixel domain but fail to address the underlying physical causes of underwater degradation. Physics-driven methods (Jaffe, 1990, Drews et al., 2016, Peng and Cosman, 2017) model the underwater imaging formation process and estimate parameters such as background light and transmission maps. Prior-based approaches (He et al., 2010, Li et al., 2016, Wang et al., 2017, Zhou et al., 2018) construct enhancement rules based on statistical image priors. While these methods offer high interpretability and computational efficiency, their performance is fundamentally constrained by manually designed paradigms. Parameter estimation errors, invalid priors under complex conditions, and poor generalization capabilities limit their applicability in real-world scenarios.

The advent of deep learning has significantly advanced the field of UIE. Data-driven methods learn complex nonlinear mappings from large-scale paired datasets, achieving superior performance without extensive parameter estimation. Various network architectures have been explored, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) (Liu et al., 2019, Karthikeyan et al., 2025, Mu et al., 2023), Transformers (Zhang et al., 2024, Zamir et al., 2022), and generative adversarial networks (GANs) (Lai et al., 2023). Recent studies have also explored spatial-frequency interaction mechanisms to improve restoration quality (Guan et al., 2026). Despite these advances, existing deep learning methods still face critical limitations. First, most methods adopt a single-branch architecture that processes color and structural information in the same feature space. This forces the model to compromise between chromatic correction and structural recovery, as these two objectives often conflict during optimization. Second, multi-scale features are typically fused using static weights or simple concatenation, leading to suboptimal recovery of fine-grained details. Third, few methods explicitly distinguish between low-frequency and high-frequency components during enhancement, making it difficult to suppress foggy artifacts while simultaneously recovering sharp textures. Fourth, although some multi-branch designs have been proposed, their feature fusion mechanisms fail to adequately exploit complementary information between branches, resulting in feature interference and suboptimal integration.

Different from existing multi-branch approaches that rely on simple concatenation or static fusion, our novelty lies in a bidirectional dynamic fusion strategy with mutual attention and learnable gating, which adaptively integrates complementary information without cross-domain interference.

To address these limitations, we propose the Underwater Dual-branch High-frequency Enhancement Network (UDHE), a lightweight architecture that explicitly decouples color restoration from structural recovery. The network processes the degraded RGB image and its corresponding grayscale representation in parallel. The grayscale image provides structural and illumination priors that are inherently free from chromatic biases, effectively decoupling structural gradient learning from color correction. While the grayscale representation inevitably inherits overall intensity attenuation from its RGB-derived computation, its primary role is to eliminate the optimization conflict between chromatic correction and structural recovery—a trade-off that severely hampers single-branch approaches. This design allows the RGB branch to focus on color restoration without compromising edge sharpness, while the grayscale branch provides unambiguous structural cues.

Our UDHE incorporates three core modules. The Efficient Residual Block (ERB) employs a wavelet-based frequency bypass that decomposes features into subbands using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). By discarding the low-frequency component and amplifying the three high-frequency subbands (HL, LH, HH), ERB explicitly enhances attenuated edges and textures. The Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) module guides high-resolution shallow features using low-resolution deep semantic features, ensuring that restored local textures remain semantically consistent with the global scene. The Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion Module (BDFM) employs a mutual attention mechanism for feature calibration and a dynamic gating mechanism for adaptive fusion. Instead of naive concatenation or weighted summation, BDFM allows the network to adaptively select clean color information in well-lit regions and rely on grayscale structural cues in heavily degraded regions, effectively preventing cross-domain interference.

For network optimization, we design a hybrid loss function that combines weighted color channel-specific L1 loss ($c{l}_{1}$) (Pramanick et al., 2025), SSIM loss (Wang et al., 2004), perceptual loss (Johnson et al., 2016), and unpaired contrastive loss (${l}_{UCR}$) (Zhou et al., 2024). This composite loss provides multi-level supervision from low-level pixel fidelity to high-level semantic consistency.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  * •

We propose UDHE, a novel dual-branch underwater image enhancement network that explicitly decouples color and structure via parallel RGB-grayscale processing, distinguishing itself from existing multi-branch methods that rely on simple concatenation or static fusion. The grayscale branch provides structural priors free from chromatic biases, effectively resolving the inherent optimization conflict between chromatic correction and structural recovery that plagues single-branch architectures.

  * •

We design three specialized modules: ERB with wavelet-based frequency bypass for explicit high-frequency compensation, CSA for semantic-guided multi-scale feature alignment, and BDFM with mutual attention and dynamic gating for adaptive cross-domain feature integration.

  * •

We formulate a hybrid loss function combining $c{l}_{1}$ loss, SSIM loss, perceptual loss, and ${l}_{UCR}$ loss, providing supervision from low-level textures to high-level semantics.

  * •

Extensive experiments on UIEB (C. Li et al., 2019), U45, UCCS (Liu et al., 2020), and LU100 (Zhou et al., 2025) datasets demonstrate that UDHE achieves competitive performance with only 0.499M parameters and an inference speed of 72 FPS. On the UIEB-T90 dataset, UDHE achieves a PSNR of 23.97 dB and SSIM of 0.9154, outperforming existing methods while satisfying real-time processing requirements.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related works. Section 3 details the proposed methodology. Section 4 presents experimental results and analysis. Section 5 concludes the paper.

# A Two-Stage Exposure Controllable Network for Image Enhancement With Low-Light Degradation

Lei Liang, Zhihua Chen, Lei Dai, Ruoxin Chen, Y.c. Zhang, Xufeng He

IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement 2025 · DOI

Bookmark

## Abstract

Controllable low-light enhancement is beneficial to both image aesthetics and high-level vision tasks. Existing methods fail to generate smooth brightness transitions with low cost. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised two-stage exposure controllable network (TSECN) featuring low-cost and natural brightness customization. Conditioning on a color-correlation based exposure reference map (CERM), an offline naturalness-preserving exposure controller (ONEC) is implemented by modulating a latent scene illumination representation, which is predicted via a two-stage progressive enhancement pipeline (TPE). Specifically, the first stage performs unsupervised low-light denoising and improves visibility with deep gamma correction. The latter handles fine-grained quality refinement and representation learning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the superior performance of our method across eight real-world datasets. On three paired datasets, TSECN outperforms advanced methods by an average PSNR improvement of 2.29 dB. Experiments on two high-level vision tasks also validate its value in application-oriented scenarios. The code will be available at https://github.com/cherrysherryplus/TSECN.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# DCD-UIE: Decoupled Chromatic Diffusion Model for Underwater Image Enhancement.

Guodong Fan, Yu Zhou, Jingchun Zhou, Yakun Ju, Guang-Yong Chen, Jinjiang Li, Alex C Kot

IEEE Transactions on Image Processing : a Publication of the IEEE Signal Processing Society 2026 January 12

Color distortion and structural degradation in underwater images are classic challenges in underwater image enhancement (UIE). The core goal is to restore degraded images to high-quality images with both color and structure that conform to visual perception. However, in the traditional RGB space, these two issues are highly coupled, resulting in existing enhancement methods often neglecting one over the other. To address this challenge, we propose a guided diffusion model based on the principle of decoupling. Our key insight is that in perceptual color spaces such as HSV, color (H, S) and structure (V) are naturally separated. To exploit this property, we first design an adaptive perceptual guidance module (APGM), which analyzes the degraded HSV image and generates two orthogonal guidance signals: a color guide and a structure guide, which guide the denoising process of the diffusion model. To ensure that this decoupled guidance is faithfully implemented, we propose a corresponding decoupled loss optimization module, which uses independent loss functions to supervise the final output color and structure. By combining the forward decoupled guidance with the backward decoupled supervision, we construct a closed-loop optimization framework. This framework enables the model to collaboratively optimize color and structure under various degradation scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in a variety of underwater scenes, particularly those degraded by color casts and haze. Furthermore, it exhibits superior performance on no-reference image quality assessment metrics. The source code is available at https://github.com/zy-world/DCD-UIE.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

王占山和程鑫彬团队联合山东师范大学在《智能光学》发表单透镜红外计算成像研究成果——检测门控自适应感兴趣区域重建方法

红外成像在夜间和弱光条件下具有应用优势，广泛应用于无人机、自动驾驶和安全监控等领域。计算成像通过引入算法提供额外的像差校正能力，为简化光学硬件、实现轻量化红外成像创造了条件。为减少先重建整幅图像再检测带来的计算开销，重建识别一体化探测方法利用重建监督辅助检测，使网络能够直接从退化图像中检测目标。然而，仅执行检测分支时，系统虽然能够输出目标位置和类别，却不提供用于人工确认的清晰目标图像。

针对这一问题，同济大学物理科学与工程学院精密光学工程技术研究所团队联合山东师范大学，提出检测门控自适应感兴趣区域重建方法（Detection-Gated Adaptive Region-of-Interest Reconstruction，DG-ROI Recon）。该方法利用检测结果引导目标区域的按需恢复，减少无关背景的冗余重建计算，兼顾目标视觉质量与处理效率。相关成果以“Detection-Gated Adaptive Region-of-Interest Reconstruction for Single-Lens Infrared Computational Imaging”为题，发表于计算成像领域新刊《智能光学》（iOptics）。

该研究从信息提取角度重新审视图像重建与目标检测的关系：当退化图像仍保留足够的定位线索时，目标检测并不总是需要以完整的全画幅重建为前提；当检测目标需要进一步人工确认时，也可以只恢复相应局部区域，从而减少背景区域的冗余计算。

DG-ROI Recon首先在退化红外图像上执行目标检测，并将检测框作为后续重建的门控信号。针对不同尺度目标，方法通过自适应尺寸分桶选择重建区域，并结合点扩散函数作用范围保留必要的上下文信息。重建完成后，利用光晕感知融合策略将局部结果平滑映射回原图；对于超过预设尺寸的目标，则自动切换至全画幅重建。
